items.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4B-parameter looped transformer model optimized for local laptop use and agentic reasoning tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Inkling 2 Mini
items.summary:
Thinking Machines has launched Inkling 2 Mini, a compact looped transformer model with 26.4 billion parameters designed to run efficiently on consumer laptops and desktops. The model applies its middle layers multiple times per token to enhance reasoning quality, outperforming other open-weight models under 100 billion parameters on benchmarks like DeepSWE v1.1 and Vals Index v2.2, while maintaining a memory footprint of about 20GB.

Inkling 2 Mini excels in agentic coding and long-horizon reasoning tasks, leading similar-sized models on several benchmarks and demonstrating improved performance with increased looping passes. It balances reasoning capabilities with efficient energy use, making it suitable for running multiple persistent AI agents locally. However, it is less effective on multi-turn chat and instruction-heavy tasks compared to larger models. The model is available with open weights on the Tinker platform for inference and customization.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate a 27B parameter language model that rewrites its own weights to improve accuracy without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.summary: A new study shows that a large language model can self-optimize by rewriting its own weights through reasoning, improving its accuracy on unseen problems by 6.6 points without gradient updates or additional training. The model tests its edits iteratively, only applying changes that enhance performance, and can repair a damaged copy of itself to regain over 80% of original accuracy on image tasks it never encountered before. This self-rewriting ability emerges only at larger scales and operates solely through forward passes, blurring the line between training and inference. The researchers suggest this approach could enable continuous self-improvement without external retraining or prompt engineering.

items.title: Anthropic shares fall 12% on second trading day amid AI sector sell-off, dragging Nasdaq down and wiping out 2026 gains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day
items.summary:
Anthropic's shares dropped by as much as 12% on their second day of trading, falling close to their IPO price, as a broader sell-off in AI-related stocks pressured the Nasdaq and other technology indices. The initial surge in Anthropic's stock on its debut was followed by a sharp decline, reflecting investor concerns about valuations and profitability in the AI sector.

The sell-off extended globally, with Asian markets experiencing their worst week since 2020, led by declines in major chipmakers and tech investors like SoftBank. Analysts noted that Anthropic's IPO may have drained liquidity from other tech stocks as investors reallocated funds. The downturn also coincided with regulatory scrutiny of companies like Nvidia and broader market worries about interest rate hikes and inflation.

This market turbulence highlights growing skepticism about the sustainability of heavy investments in AI and technology, as investors question whether these companies can deliver the expected returns amid elevated valuations and economic uncertainties.

items.title: Engineer uses AI coding agents to program an FPGA for running a large language model, achieving a 33× speedup to 213 tokens per second [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Vibecoding an inference chip
items.summary:
An engineer experimented with programming an FPGA to run a large language model (LLM) using AI coding agents, achieving a significant performance improvement. By leveraging cloud-based FPGA instances and AI models like Codex, Astra, and Opus, the project progressed from initial functionality to real-time inference speeds with minimal direct human coding.

The process involved running extensive automated experiments over several days, generating millions of lines of code and output analysis while spending around $10,000 on AI tokens. The engineer combined AI-driven code generation with occasional expert guidance, resulting in a 33-fold speed increase from the baseline to 213 tokens per second. This work demonstrates the potential of AI-assisted development for hardware programming and AI inference acceleration on reprogrammable chips.

items.title: Researchers develop PsyWorld, a profile-conditioned state world model using transition-informed representations to improve human behavior prediction and generalize to unseen individuals
items.originalTitle: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
items.summary: Researchers have introduced PsyWorld, a profile-conditioned state world model that integrates stable psychometric traits with observed environment-behavior state transitions to enhance human behavior prediction. Unlike traditional models that condition actions solely on static profiles, PsyWorld uses transition-informed representations learned through a posterior encoder and prior predictor to better capture behavioral dynamics. Evaluations in simulated environments with participant-disjoint splits demonstrated high accuracy and improved generalization to unseen individuals, establishing the value of transition supervision in behavioral modeling without implying causal psychological mechanisms or long-term state calibration.

items.title: Researchers introduce LR-Merge to predict and correct interference in multi-task model merging using directional derivatives and surrogate affine models, improving efficiency and accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
items.summary: A new study presents LR-Merge, a method that predicts and corrects interference when merging separately fine-tuned models by evaluating first-order directional derivatives at the receiver model. This approach reduces computational costs by optimizing merge coefficients without backpropagation and improves performance across various base mergers, especially as more tasks are combined. The method outperforms alternatives relying on pretrained responses and matches the accuracy of exact teacher matching with lower compute requirements. LR-Merge uses a surrogate affine model to efficiently handle coefficient and task-subset queries, enabling faster and more scalable multi-task model merging.

items.originalSummary: A new study introduces LR-Merge, a method to improve model merging by predicting and correcting interference between tasks. Traditional approaches assess interference only after merging models, which is computationally expensive. The researchers demonstrate that evaluating a first-order directional derivative at the receiver model can predict interference and identify prediction changes more effectively. For multi-task merges, two evaluations along the merge path are necessary. LR-Merge uses a surrogate affine model to optimize merge coefficients without backpropagation, enhancing performance across various base mergers and scaling well with the number of tasks. This approach outperforms methods relying on pretrained responses and matches the accuracy of exact teacher matching with less computational cost.

items.title: Researchers propose Density Feedback Control to improve transferability and target density accuracy of generative sparse adversarial attacks on CNN and Transformer models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Density Feedback Control for Transferability of Generative Sparse Adversarial Attacks
items.summary: Researchers have introduced Density Feedback Control (DFC), a method that dynamically adjusts the sparsity coefficient in generator-based sparse adversarial attacks to better achieve target perturbation densities and enhance transfer attack success rates. Unlike traditional fixed-coefficient approaches, DFC modifies the coefficient based on the difference between observed and target densities without changing the generator's architecture or loss function. Experiments demonstrate that DFC achieves target densities within one percentage point and improves attack success rates on CNN and Transformer models while perturbing fewer pixels. However, when attacks are restricted to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC does not consistently improve performance, indicating complex interactions between such restrictions and density feedback.

items.originalSummary: A new method called Density Feedback Control (DFC) has been introduced to improve generator-based sparse adversarial attacks, which are used to evaluate the robustness of black-box models. Traditional approaches set perturbation density indirectly through a fixed sparsity coefficient, making it difficult to achieve target densities and limiting transferability gains. DFC dynamically adjusts this coefficient based on the difference between observed and target perturbation densities, without altering the generator's architecture or loss function. Experiments show that DFC effectively achieves target densities and enhances transfer attack success rates on CNN and Transformer models while perturbing fewer pixels. However, for attacks restricted to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC does not consistently improve performance, highlighting interactions between such restrictions and density feedback.

items.summary: Researchers have introduced PoolDPP, a method that enhances diversity in language model outputs by sampling subsets of strings using determinantal point processes (DPPs), which balance item quality and repulsion between similar outputs. PoolDPP generates a candidate pool, reweights samples, and selects diverse subsets with theoretical bounds on its approximation quality. Empirical evaluations show that PoolDPP improves diversity and quality trade-offs in open-ended text generation, ambiguous text-to-SQL translation, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

items.title: Study analyzes impact of feature reduction techniques on adversarial robustness of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal perturbation attacks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
items.summary: Researchers evaluated how different feature reduction methods affect the adversarial robustness of various machine learning classifiers, including support vector machines, decision trees, random forests, multi-layer perceptrons, and k-nearest neighbors, using the APT dataset. The study compared principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information, measuring outcomes with accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation scores. Results showed that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally improved robustness more consistently, while other techniques had variable effects depending on the classifier and attack type.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

items.title: Researchers construct a near-quadratic sample compression scheme of size O(d² log² d) for all VC dimension d classes, proving the weaker sample compression conjecture [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
items.summary: The sample compression conjecture, a longstanding open problem in learning theory since the 1980s, posits that every binary concept class with VC dimension d admits a sample compression scheme of size proportional to d. While the original conjecture remains unresolved, researchers have now proven the weaker version by developing a sample compression scheme with size O(d² log² d). This result advances understanding of the relationship between simplification and generalization in machine learning by showing that predictors consistent with training samples can be defined using a polynomially bounded subset of the data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way. The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.

items.title: Researchers propose HapBO, a Bayesian Optimization method using expert natural language priors compiled into reusable belief functions, improving sample efficiency without in-loop LLM calls [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HapBO: Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
items.summary:
Researchers introduce HapBO (Harnessed α-π Bayesian Optimization), which converts expert knowledge expressed in natural language into structured belief functions to guide Bayesian Optimization (BO). HapBO applies these beliefs as bounded multipliers on acquisition functions, preserving optimization performance without requiring repeated large language model (LLM) calls during the process. The method supports rich belief representations beyond Gaussian assumptions and maintains regret bounds even under adversarial beliefs.

HapBO was evaluated on 40 HPOBench tasks, synthetic benchmarks in 6-15 dimensions, and real-world problems including cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. It achieved the lowest aggregate regret on HPOBench and improved outcomes in real-world tasks with query budgets of 12-20, while incurring minimal wall-clock time and token costs compared to other LLM-based approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($\pi: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $\alpha$-$\pi$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

items.title: Researchers release a long-range video face presentation attack detection dataset spanning 1-100 meters with two sensor types and benchmark CNN models for three-class classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Long-Range Video Presentation Attack Detection: A Three-Class Benchmark Across 1-100 m and Two Sensor Types
items.summary: Researchers have introduced a new video-based face presentation attack detection (PAD) dataset comprising over 374,000 frames from 261 individuals captured at distances from 1 to 100 meters using a DSLR camera and a mobile sensor. The dataset includes three-class labels—live, spoof, and props (occlusions)—and is designed to address challenges in multi-distance capture and diverse environmental conditions that current PAD systems, typically limited to close-range detection, do not cover. Four convolutional neural network architectures were fine-tuned and benchmarked, with EfficientNet achieving the highest accuracy of 98.48% and an ACER of 2.01%.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) systems deployed in border control and airport surveillance are constrained by a critical assumption: subjects are captured at close range, typically under one meter. No existing benchmark systematically addresses multi-distance capture, diverse environmental conditions, and concurrent spoofing and occlusion-based attacks, leaving deployed models underprepared for real-world scenarios. We introduce a video-based PAD dataset of 374,000+ frames from 261 unique identities collected across five standoff distances (1 m-100 m) under indoor and outdoor conditions using a DSLR camera (C) and a mobile sensor (M), with three-class labels: live, spoof, and props (occlusions); models are trained and evaluated on video clips rather than single frames. We fine-tune and benchmark four CNN architectures: MobileNetV3, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ResNet-50. The higher-resolution DSLR maintains near-perfect spoof classification rate across all distances, while the lower-resolution mobile sensor degrades sharply beyond 50 m, with props classification rate dropping to 55% at 75 m for MobileNetV3. EfficientNet achieves the best overall performance (98.48% accuracy, ACER 2.01%). Generalization tests on unseen attack datasets yield 89-94% accuracy, validating cross-domain robustness. These results establish capture distance and sensor resolution as critical but underexplored axes of PAD difficulty. The dataset will be publicly released under an End-User License Agreement to support reproducible long-range PAD research.

items.title: discoCVI package releases memory-efficient R implementation of DISCO index for density-based clustering evaluation, achieving up to 138x speedup and linear memory growth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
items.summary: The discoCVI package introduces a new R implementation of the DISCO internal cluster validity index, designed for density-based clustering and noise label evaluation. This version computes the index using the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, reducing memory usage to grow linearly with data size while maintaining quadratic runtime. Benchmarks show the implementation is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous R version for datasets of 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for up to 8,000 points, using significantly less memory and scoring 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with under 200 MB of memory.

Benchmarks show the implementation is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous R version for datasets of 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for up to 8,000 points, using significantly less memory and scoring 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with under 200 MB of memory.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.

items.title: Researchers audit DeepMind's GraphCast weather model using sparse autoencoder features to test causal relevance and improve extreme-event forecasts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
items.summary: Researchers analyzed internal representations of DeepMind's GraphCast, an autoregressive weather forecasting model, to determine if causal relevance requires physical semantics. They applied interventions to the model's internal activations during rollout to assess the impact on forecast accuracy, particularly for extreme events like tropical cyclones. Ablating a feature tied to the model's computational mesh increased global geopotential height error despite lacking clear physical meaning, while manipulating features associated with convection and low-level vorticity affected tropical cyclone intensity predictions. Amplifying convection-related features reduced intensity error by a median of 51% across seven storms. These findings distinguish physical interpretability from causal utility and demonstrate that sparse features can serve as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening in learned weather dynamics.

They applied interventions to the model's internal activations during rollout to assess the impact on forecast accuracy, particularly for extreme events like tropical cyclones. Ablating a feature tied to the model's computational mesh increased global geopotential height error despite lacking clear physical meaning, while manipulating features associated with convection and low-level vorticity affected tropical cyclone intensity predictions. Amplifying convection-related features reduced intensity error by a median of 51% across seven storms. These findings distinguish physical interpretability from causal utility and demonstrate that sparse features can serve as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening in learned weather dynamics.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learned weather models are experimentally accessible computational systems whose internal representations can be inspected and manipulated. Using sparse autoencoder features from GraphCast, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model, we test whether causal relevance requires physical semantics, a question that matters for auditing whether AI forecasters used in high-assurance settings rely on reliable mechanisms. We also look at whether physically associated latent directions can be steered to improve extreme-event forecasts, where interventions are applied to the model's internal activations during the rollout. We find that ablating a feature locked to GraphCast's computational mesh increases global geopotential height error despite lacking conventional physical semantics. Second, suppressing convection- and low-level-vorticity-associated features weakens predicted tropical-cyclone deepening (the fall in central pressure during intensification), while amplifying them reduces intensity error, with amplification of convection features through feature scaling achieving a median of 51\% error reduction over seven storms. Together, these results separate interpretable, physical association from causal utility and establish sparse features as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening on learned weather dynamics.

items.title: Researchers develop coupled neural operator framework for temporal extrapolation of elastic seismic wave propagation in layered media with stress conditioning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Temporal Extrapolation of Elastic Seismic Wave Propagation in Layered Media Using Neural Operators
items.summary: Researchers have developed a coupled neural operator framework combining a time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network and a Fourier Neural Operator to predict seismic velocity fields beyond training intervals in layered elastic media. The model uses a predictor-corrector approach with reference velocity and stress fields to autoregressively forecast horizontally polarized shear waves in layered soil columns with varying depths and properties. Evaluations show the model reproduces key velocity arrivals and depth-dependent responses with mean normalized root-mean-square errors between 0.53% and 2.82% over extrapolation intervals. While the framework demonstrates effective temporal velocity prediction under stress conditioning, autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal prediction of seismic velocity fields beyond the time interval represented in training remains challenging for neural operator models. This study develops a coupled neural operator framework for stress-conditioned temporal prediction in layered elastic media. A time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network (TI-DeepONet) advances the velocity field through an embedded fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) scheme, while a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learns a residual correction to the predicted spatial field. The two components are trained jointly in a predictor-corrector configuration. Prediction is initialized with reference velocity fields at the first two time levels and proceeds autoregressively, with reference stress fields and prescribed excitation supplied throughout rollout, including beyond the training interval. Four cases consider horizontally polarized shear (SH) waves in four-layer soil columns with fixed total depths of 50 and 280 m, excited by third-order Gaussian-derivative (DOG3) wavelets with central frequencies between 0.5 and 6 Hz. Layer thicknesses and shear-wave velocities vary across profiles. Evaluations on test profiles extend beyond the training interval by up to twice its duration. The predictions reproduce principal velocity arrivals and depth-dependent response patterns, with accuracy varying across profiles. Across the four cases, mean peak-normalized root-mean-square errors (NRMSEs) range from 0.53% to 2.31% over the full evaluation windows and from 0.61% to 2.82% over the extrapolation intervals. Both metrics use each profile's peak absolute reference velocity over the full evaluation window as the normalizer. These results demonstrate temporal velocity prediction under reference-stress conditioning for the tested configurations; autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.

items.title: Researchers propose a rate-distortion framework for hierarchical content summarization to quantitatively assess generative model performance in long-context question-answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rate-distortion Assessment for Hierarchical Content Summarization
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a framework inspired by Shannon's rate-distortion theory to formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem. This approach extracts semantic hierarchies from source content to measure the trade-off between compression efficiency and information loss during generative content manipulation, enabling benchmarking of models based on rate budgets.

The framework is demonstrated through experiments with state-of-the-art large language models on long-context question-answering tasks, providing insights into their efficiency and comprehension. Additionally, the semantic hierarchy guides retrieval-augmented generation, improving rate-distortion performance compared to existing baselines.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Powerful generative models including large language and vision models have demonstrated success across a wide range of content generation, editing and manipulation tasks via end-to-end prompt-based generation. However, current assessment of the quality of generative content manipulation remains subjective, limiting scientific understanding of model capabilities. Inspired by rate-distortion theory from Shannon information compression theory, in this work we formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem. We design a principled framework to extract the semantic hierarchy of the source content to support quantitative characterization of the rate-distortion trade-off between compression efficiency (rate) against information loss (distortion) during generative content manipulation, which allows us to benchmark various models with respect to performance conditional on rate budget of interest. We demonstrate the use of the framework with empirical experiments on content summarization for long-context question-answering with state-of-the-art large language models, offering new insights into their efficiency and comprehension capabilities. We further demonstrate the use of the semantic hierarchy as guidance for performing effective retrieval augmented generation, showing improved rate-distortion characteristics against current baselines.

items.title: Researchers develop Bayesian κ-Explorer for minimax transition estimation in unknown MDPs, simplifying exploration with Dirichlet priors and achieving comparable convergence rates to frequentist methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer for Minimax Model Estimation in MDPs
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Bayesian κ-Explorer, an algorithm for active exploration in minimax transition estimation within unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs). By applying Dirichlet priors to transition distributions, the method simplifies the exploration process by using the posterior mean model and eliminating the need for confidence-set optimization, while maintaining a surrogate convergence rate of approximately T^{-1/3} similar to frequentist κ-Explorer.

The approach leverages the posterior expected squared ℓ2 error equaling total posterior variance to provide a closed-form exploration signal. The team also establishes bounds on the maximum posterior variance relative to the optimal asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark. Experimental results on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi environments demonstrate that Bayesian κ-Explorer achieves lower worst-case transition-estimation errors compared to baseline methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study active exploration for minimax transition estimation in unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs). Frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer~\citep{gu2026kappa} addresses this problem through a parameterized family of exploration objectives, but requires confidence-bound constructions and joint optimization over plausible transition kernels and occupancy measures, introducing a computational burden that limits its practical applicability. We develop Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer, which simplifies this procedure by placing Dirichlet priors on the transition distributions. Under the posterior mean estimator, the posterior expected squared $\ell_2$ error equals the total posterior variance, providing a closed-form exploration signal. The algorithm plans under the posterior mean model, eliminating confidence-set optimization. Under the stated assumptions, this simpler planning procedure retains the $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/3})$ surrogate convergence rate of frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer. We further bound the maximum posterior variance relative to the optimal asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark. Experiments on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi demonstrate lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than the tested baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose DualSAE framework to separate interpretability and reconstruction in sparse autoencoders, improving reconstruction fidelity by 29% and interpretability by 34% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary: Researchers introduce DualSAE, a modular framework that augments traditional sparse autoencoders with a Residual Branch to separate semantic interpretability from reconstruction fidelity. The Sparse Branch captures dominant semantic features, while the Residual Branch models non-semantic information, with a decorrelation loss minimizing overlap between them. DualSAE uses a two-stage training strategy and demonstrates improvements across vision and language datasets. The approach enhances downstream tasks such as topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and large language model steering by providing more interpretable representations without sacrificing reconstruction quality.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.

items.title: Researchers introduce InflEns, a game-theoretic mixture of LoRA experts that uses training data allocation to predict expert specialization and guide inference without explicit gating [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Game-Theoretic Data Allocation for Expert Specialization and Routing
items.summary:
Researchers present InflEns, a framework that models expert training and routing as a location game in a fixed prompt-trait space, allowing the allocation used for training to predict which expert performs best on a given prompt. Evaluated on seven safety-related benchmarks, InflEns shows that the expert with the highest share of prompts achieves the lowest negative log-likelihood on about 90% of prompts, outperforming random allocation and matching learned gating methods without training an explicit gate.

The fixed routing mechanism enables tracing harmful behavior to individual experts, allowing targeted retraining that significantly reduces attack success rates while maintaining instruction following. InflEns offers controls over expert specialization through kernel choice, trait-space geometry, and expert count, and is designed as a general framework extendable to any encoder and data distribution.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.

items.title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. items.title: {\phi}TD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: {\phi}TD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.

items.title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. We study products of permutations of five items, a task that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve on all input lengths under the standard conjecture that $\mathrm{TC}^0 \ne \mathrm{NC}^1$. On two-event windows, a 27B model answered 3 of 100 correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 when it generated intermediate steps. A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each. The same package passed 298 of 299 new windows on a fresh machine, missing the target of 0.99 for the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. A separate follow-up sized to allow one failure yielded 472 of 473. On 1,000-event room-swap documents, three of ten models solved all five documents by reasoning alone. All seven models tested both ways at this length solved all five with extraction and the register, with no chain of thought requested. With concurrent extraction, median wall-clock time fell from 136.1 to 10.4 s for Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s for GPT-6.1 Sol. At fixed per-token rates, mean cost per document fell by 55% for Sonnet 5.5 and 44% for GPT-6.1 Sol. A regular expression with an executor also solved all 15 fixed-format documents. On 500 free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader identified the recorded value in 68.8% of cases, compared with 61.0% for a frequency baseline fitted on the same training projects.

items.title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.

items.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.

items.title: Process-Knowledge-Guided Latent Diffusion for Generative Design of Porous Architectures: A Case Study in Aerosol Jet Printing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Process-Knowledge-Guided Latent Diffusion for Generative Design of Porous Architectures: A Case Study in Aerosol Jet Printing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Printed porous layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the layout that uses the material best depends on how the process settings shape the deposit. Generative models propose layouts quickly, but a generator that does not receive the process setting samples from the same distribution at every setting, even when the process-dependent score ranks candidate layouts differently. This paper examines whether process knowledge can steer a latent diffusion generator toward layouts suited to a given process setting in a prescribed design domain. We formulate a process-dependent utilization score in which a process model sets the length over which the utility of printed material decays with distance from a channel. The generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent representation, a topology U-Net, a ControlNet domain branch, and a separately trained regressor that predicts the score from noised latents; the domain branch conditions each denoising step and the regressor gradient steers it. The method is applied to aerosol jet printing, where the atomizer and sheath gas flows enter the score through the flow-focusing relation. Across seven modeled flow settings, the lowest-scoring candidate layout of a domain differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains. In a sampling study, the mean directly computed score on three validation domains and one test domain was 0.642 with domain conditioning alone, 0.636 at a weight of 300, and 0.450 at 12,000 (112 scores per weight; lower is better). The results support process-knowledge-guided generation as an approach to process-specific porous design under the stated assumptions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Printed porous layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the layout that uses the material best depends on how the process settings shape the deposit. Generative models propose layouts quickly, but a generator that does not receive the process setting samples from the same distribution at every setting, even when the process-dependent score ranks candidate layouts differently. This paper examines whether process knowledge can steer a latent diffusion generator toward layouts suited to a given process setting in a prescribed design domain. We formulate a process-dependent utilization score in which a process model sets the length over which the utility of printed material decays with distance from a channel. The generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent representation, a topology U-Net, a ControlNet domain branch, and a separately trained regressor that predicts the score from noised latents; the domain branch conditions each denoising step and the regressor gradient steers it. The method is applied to aerosol jet printing, where the atomizer and sheath gas flows enter the score through the flow-focusing relation. Across seven modeled flow settings, the lowest-scoring candidate layout of a domain differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains. In a sampling study, the mean directly computed score on three validation domains and one test domain was 0.642 with domain conditioning alone, 0.636 at a weight of 300, and 0.450 at 12,000 (112 scores per weight; lower is better). The results support process-knowledge-guided generation as an approach to process-specific porous design under the stated assumptions.

items.title: Learning to Verify: Signature-Guided Training for Adaptive Adversarial Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Verify: Signature-Guided Training for Adaptive Adversarial Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial example detectors often fail when attackers explicitly attempt to bypass them. We propose a dual-model approach that keeps the original classifier fixed and trains a separate verifier to assess its predictions. During training, we identify patterns of internal neural network activations that distinguish genuine examples of each class from adversarial examples targeting that class. These patterns, called activation signatures, guide the generation of challenging adversarial examples that mislead the classifier, challenge the verifier, and internally resemble the target class. The verifier learns to recognize these examples while preserving its performance on clean inputs through knowledge distillation. At inference, the verifier evaluates the classifier's prediction without requiring activation signatures. We evaluate the approach on publicly available datasets against several adaptive attacks, including attacks unseen during training. The proposed verifier substantially outperforms directly attacked confidence-based and feature-based detectors under the evaluated L-infinity attacks. Ablation studies show that adaptive verifier training is the main source of this improvement, while signature guidance primarily benefits clean accuracy. Additional L2 evaluations reveal limitations in robustness across perturbation types.

items.title: Scone: Symmetry-aware Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Graph Coloring [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Scone: Symmetry-aware Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Graph Coloring
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph coloring, which entails assigning colors to nodes such that no adjacent nodes have the same color, is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem. In general, however, finding a node coloring with no monochromatic edges given a fixed palette is NP-hard. This motivates learning-based methods that can learn to exploit recurring structure across instances to efficiently produce high-quality colorings. Crucially, the validity of a coloring is invariant to permutations of the colors, and we show that exploiting this symmetry reduces the size of the effective state space over which the model has to learn its policy. At the same time, the coloring algorithm must be able to break some symmetries, for example to assign different colors to two adjacent nodes belonging to the same automorphism orbit. In this paper, we introduce Scone, a model that uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to construct colorings sequentially, allowing information from previous assignments to propagate and break node symmetries. Scone achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks, including on sudoku_extreme and register allocations, and showcases generalization to graph families not encountered during training.

items.title: DS3M: Deep structured state space models for nonlinear system identification on modern hardware [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DS3M: Deep structured state space models for nonlinear system identification on modern hardware
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

items.title: Intelligent Embedding Pruning for Large-Scale Recommendation Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Intelligent Embedding Pruning for Large-Scale Recommendation Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.

items.title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.

items.title: Federated Learning of Car Aerodynamics Surrogates with Spectral Optimizers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Federated Learning of Car Aerodynamics Surrogates with Spectral Optimizers
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural surrogates predict the aerodynamic forces on a car in seconds, compared with hours for a CFD simulation, but training them requires thousands of CFD simulations of different car designs, which car manufacturers keep proprietary. Federated learning allows several manufacturers to train a shared surrogate without exchanging data. We study which federated optimizer brings such a surrogate closest to one trained on pooled data. On DrivAerNet++, we train a Transolver surrogate across six clients that each hold cars of a single body type, and we compare three spectral optimizers, which orthogonalize the update of each weight matrix (FedMuon and two methods we propose, FedMARS-M and FedOLion), with three non-spectral ones (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam and FedLion), all tuned with the same protocol. FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized training with Muon, using two to four local epochs per round. The non-spectral methods perform best with sixteen local epochs, the largest number we tested, and still have a 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M. We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step yields about twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm. items.title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.

items.title: Prescribed Bayesian Efficiency under Lifetime Adjustment Costs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Prescribed Bayesian Efficiency under Lifetime Adjustment Costs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Bayesian learner may retain an issued action while updating its posterior, trading predictive loss against adjustment charges. We assume population curvature, boundary control, an order-$1/n$ lower bound on expected posterior uncertainty about the optimal action, and an observable unbiased gradient witness whose squared norms are uniformly integrable. Sample losses may be unbounded or nonconvex. Cumulative expected excess measures the loss increase relative to current predictive Bayes actions. For bounded nonnegative nondecreasing charges $c$ with $c(0)=0$ and nondecreasing profiles $G: \mathbb{N} \to [1,\infty)$ with $G(J)=o(J)$, we characterize joint attainability of cumulative expected excess $O(G(J))$ at horizons $T=2^J$ and finite expected lifetime charge. Here $J$ indexes logarithmic time. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, equivalently its decreasing-weight dual. Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For each feasible pair, a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy attains the profile with lifetime-cost moments of every positive order. For excess $O((\log T)^r)$, $0<r<1$, every policy needs $\Omega((\log T)^{2-r})$ revisions in expectation, and a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound for every feasible charge. We verify the assumptions for logistic decision models with nondegenerate covariates, finite second moments and a locally positive smooth prior density, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors.

items.title: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25320v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.

items.title: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In regulated domains such as lending, the two most salient fairness concepts are disparate impact and disparate treatment: disparate impact is generally defined by differential rates of adverse outcomes between demographic groups, while disparate treatment is generally defined by the use of demographic information or proxies to issue decisions. There already exist established methods to quantitatively detect and mitigate disparate impact; however, there has been less research on doing the same for disparate treatment. From a practitioner's perspective, the manner in which a conditional independence test is formulated and operationalized to identify proxies is nuanced and underexplored. As Machine Learning (ML) systems increase in scope and application in regulated domains, practitioners need a defensible framework to identify proxies at scale. Current disparate treatment frameworks typically rely upon some combination of quantitative and qualitative review of models' inputs to identify proxies. Features that are identified as proxies are then typically removed from the model in practice, and predictive performance degrades in favor of fairness through unawareness. Here, we propose a two-part framework that reduces the disparate treatment risk of a feature and keeps the predictive performance that removal of the feature loses. First, we propose a quantitative test for proxy capacity that identifies whether some of a feature's values reveal membership in a particular demographic group. Second, we propose a pre-processing methodology that adjusts those proxy features to reduce their proxy capacity. We show empirically on synthetic and public datasets that this framework identifies features that proxy for demographic information and reduces their proxy capacity while the adjusted feature retains task-relevant signal (i.e. improves predictive performance versus removal).

items.title: Class-Conditional Conformal Triage for ICAO Face-Image Compliance under Class Imbalance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Class-Conditional Conformal Triage for ICAO Face-Image Compliance under Class Imbalance
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated ICAO/ISO face-image compliance analysers provide criterion-level pass/fail decisions, yet these verdicts do not quantify uncertainty when deciding whether to accept, reject, or retake a photograph. We investigate conformal prediction as a triage layer for BioGaze, evaluating 14 compliance criteria on the synthetic TONO benchmark. Without retraining the analyser, we fit per-criterion logistic classifiers and compare marginal and label-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction with conventional abstention rules using subject-disjoint splits. Marginal conformal prediction achieved approximately 0.90 overall coverage but substantially under-covered violations, with a ten-partition mean of 0.37 for one criterion. The corresponding Mondrian means ranged from 0.89 to 0.92 across criteria. However, most of the reduction in criterion-level false positives came from the logistic layer (0.145 to 0.048), while tuned abstention rules achieved lower false-positive rates than Mondrian at comparable retake rates. Bonferroni correction for joint coverage across 14 criteria required retaking nearly all images. These findings show that class-conditional conformal prediction can achieve near-target empirical coverage for minority violation classes and reveal trade-offs between statistical coverage, classification performance, and retake requirements in multi-criterion face-image compliance assessment.

items.title: Drifting, Discriminating, and Directioning for Action Coordination in Higher-dimensional Action Space [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Drifting, Discriminating, and Directioning for Action Coordination in Higher-dimensional Action Space
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a lightweight policy model to mitigate the difficulty of handling higher-dimensional action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL), alongside an algorithm to effectively train it. To address this, we focus on drifting models, which can implicitly represent complex distributions and infer actions in a single forward pass. However, while drifting models can be straightforwardly trained via backpropagation of the Q-gradient, this alone cannot be expected to appropriately capture the desired action coordination. Therefore, this paper constructs a three-step learning algorithm to encourage the action coordination. First, the source distribution of the drifting model is co-optimized as a diagonal policy model. This conditions the drifting model to attach the coordination, which cannot be expressed by a diagonal distribution, as residuals. Second, a discriminator model before and after drifting is introduced with adversarial training for a regularization term. This actively promotes the extraction of the coordination that fundamentally separates the two distributions. Third, best-of-N sampling is applied for action selection during rollouts in order to give directionality toward/beyond the regions where the coordination is insufficiently extracted/sufficiently discovered. The proposed method consistently improves the sample efficiency and the final control performance over the conventional diagonal distribution modeling across three locomotion tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that this improvement is achieved by reducing variance in certain action dimensions, effectively coupling them with other actions as action coordination.

items.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

items.title: Protein Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Protein Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are commonly pretrained with likelihood-based objectives such as masked language modeling or denoising. These objectives capture sequence-level regularities, but can produce representations in which functional signals are entangled with non-functional variation (e.g., sequence identity, compositional bias, and frequent local motifs), creating a readout bottleneck for downstream function prediction. We introduce Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification (SAVR), a contrastive post-training method using Pfam family co-membership as a homology-guided discrete semantic signal to reshape PLM representations. SAVR reduces directional dominance and redistributes variance across embedding dimensions, decreasing variance concentration, and increasing effective dimensionality of the embedding covariance spectrum. Without observing any task-specific labels during post-training, SAVR achieves state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks and competitive results on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks under frozen-backbone evaluation. These results suggest that homology-guided contrastive post-training can rectify PLM representation geometry and improve sequence-based protein function prediction.

items.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

items.title: FG-GraphBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding with Multimodal Scene Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FG-GraphBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding with Multimodal Scene Graphs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to recognize small visual entities and understand their relationships. Scene graphs offer a natural way to represent this information, organizing visual entities as nodes and their relationships as edges. However, we identify two challenges: existing scene graph benchmarks provide insufficient coverage of fine-grained entities and the relationships among them, and existing methods for fine-grained visual understanding have yet to effectively leverage such graph-structured information in MLLMs. To address these challenges, we introduce Fine-Grained Multimodal Scene Graph Benchmark (FG-GraphBench) and FiGRA. FG-GraphBench is a benchmark comprising three complementary tasks: fine-grained visual question answering (FG-QA), image captioning (FG-Caption), and image description generation (FG-Description). We develop a two-stage construction pipeline that discovers and grounds fine-grained entities and establishes their relations to construct the fine-grained multimodal scene graphs (MSGs) in FG-GraphBench. Building on these MSGs, we propose FiGRA, a Fine-grained Graph Representation Augmentation method for MLLMs. FiGRA adopts a two-stage training strategy. It encodes multimodal entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens, and integrates them into the MLLM. Experiments show that FiGRA significantly outperforms strong baselines across three tasks of FG-GraphBench. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of FG-GraphBench and highlight the importance of preserving fine-grained entity and relation information for visual understanding.
